package.title: Why Does Popcorn Pop? 4x Your Car Tire's Pressure 🍿
package.description:
Why does popcorn pop? Water inside each kernel turns to steam, pressure builds to about 135 psi behind the hard hull, and at around 180°C it bursts and the starch puffs into foam up to 40 times bigger.

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: do you eat the unpopped kernels at the bottom of the bowl, or leave them? 👇
package.script: Your popcorn explodes at about 4 times, your car tire's pressure. Every kernel hides a bit of water, about 14 percent, packed in soft starch, locked inside a hard shell called the hull. Heat it up, and that water turns to steam. But the hull barely leaks, so steam has nowhere to go. Pressure climbs to about 135 pounds per square inch. Then, at around 180 degrees Celsius, the hull cracks. The starch blasts out and puffs into foam, up to 40 times bigger. And the pop you hear? That's not the shell breaking. It's the steam escaping. The first bit of starch forms a little leg, flinging the kernel into the air. Those duds in your bowl were too dry to build pressure. So, do you eat the ones that didn't explode?
key_facts: Popcorn needs about 14% moisture to pop
Pressure reaches about 135 psi before the hull bursts (popcorn.org), roughly 4x a 30-35 psi car tire
Bursts at about 180°C
Can swell to 40-50 times its size (popcorn.org)
The pop sound comes from vapor release, not the hull cracking (Scientific American)
First starch forms a leg that catapults the kernel (popcorn.org)
Too-dry kernels don't build enough pressure

package.description:
Why does pineapple make your tongue sting? Bromelain, a mix of protein-cutting enzymes in fresh pineapple, breaks down the slimy mucus coat in your mouth, and the fruit's acid then stings the exposed spots. Heat changes the enzyme's shape, which is why canned or grilled pineapple doesn't bite.

package.pinned_comment: Would you still eat a fruit that digests your tongue? Raw, canned or grilled, which is your pick?
package.script: Pineapple digests your tongue with every bite you take. That sting on your tongue, isn't just sour. Pineapple is packed with bromelain, a mix of enzymes that chop up protein. And your tongue? It's made of protein. So while you're chewing, bromelain cuts into the slimy coat, that protects your mouth. Then the fruit's acid, around pH three to four, splashes onto the exposed spots. That's the sting. Meat tenderizer powders often use the same enzyme, so yes, your tongue is getting tenderized. But heat changes the enzyme's shape, at about seventy to eighty degrees Celsius, and it stops working. That's why canned or grilled pineapple doesn't bite. Relax, your mouth heals fast, tiny damage can fade within hours. So tell me, would you still eat a fruit that digests your tongue?
key_facts: Bromelain is a mix of protein-cutting enzymes found in pineapple; it breaks down the mucous lining and surface tissue of the mouth (Science Meets Food, Science ABC).
Acid intensifies the sting by hitting freshly exposed tissue; pineapple is about pH 3 to 4 (Science ABC, Inverse).
Powdered meat tenderizers often contain bromelain or papain (Science Meets Food).
Heat denatures bromelain; about 70 to 80 C (160 to 175 F) tames it, and canned pineapple has been heated (Inverse, Science Meets Food).
Mouth tissue heals fast; trivial damage heals within hours (Science ABC).

package.script: Your dog's wet nose traps smells you'll never notice, and it might even sense heat. That shine is a thin layer of mucus, made by tiny glands in the nose. Smells are tiny floating particles, and they stick better to damp surfaces. Then your dog licks its nose, carrying those particles into its mouth, up to a special scent organ. Dogs have over a hundred million scent receptors. You've got about six million. But here's the strange part. In twenty-twenty, scientists trained three dogs to find the warmer of two objects, from about five feet away. All three could do it. package.description:
Why does hair turn grey? Melanocyte stem cells in the hair follicle stop moving and get stuck, so fewer colour cells make melanin, a finding from a 2023 study in mice.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: If scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey or go back?
package.script: Your grey hairs start with stuck cells, tiny ones, at your roots. Hair gets its colour from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. They sit at the bottom of each follicle, and inject colour as the hair grows. But those cells need replacing, and that's the job of stem cells. In mice, scientists found these stem cells commute, moving up and down the follicle. Moving is how they get the signal to make colour. But as hair ages, more of them stop. They get stuck in a spot called the bulge. In plucked mouse hair, stuck cells jumped, from fifteen percent to nearly fifty. Stuck cells can't make new colour cells. Less melanin means grey, no melanin means white. By your early sixties, about ninety-one percent of people have some grey. So if scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey, or go back?

package.pinned_comment: Which hive job would you want: cleaner, nurse, builder, guard, or forager?
package.script: Sixty thousand bees, no boss, and you'd never guess how they run it. This hive builds perfect rooms, runs its own heating and cooling, and shares maps by dancing. So how does a honeybee hive actually work? Let's start with the queen. She sounds like the boss, but she doesn't give orders. Her real job is eggs. At her peak, she can lay up to fifteen hundred a day. That's about one egg every minute, all day and all night. Around her are a few hundred males, called drones. They're only here to mate with a new queen. And when the cold comes in fall, the workers shove them out the door. Everyone else is a worker, and every worker is female. A queen and a worker can start as the same kind of egg. The difference is food. A future queen gets loads of royal jelly, and a worker gets far less. Now, a summer worker only lives about six weeks, and she changes careers the whole way through. Day one, she's a cleaner, polishing her own cell. Around day five, she's a nurse, feeding the babies. Around day twelve, wax glands on her belly switch on, so she turns builder. Around day fifteen, she can guard the door. And after about three weeks, she finally goes outside, to spend the rest of her life hunting flowers. Wax is seriously expensive. It takes about eight pounds of honey, to make one pound of wax. So the hive can't waste a drop. Circles leave gaps. Squares and triangles fit, but they use more wall. Hexagons give you the most room, for the least wax. People suspected that for centuries, but a mathematician only proved it in nineteen ninety-nine. Bees got there first, with no math at all. Now, the coolest trick in the hive. A forager finds flowers a long way off. How does she tell her sisters, in the pitch dark, with no words? She dances. She runs in a straight line, shaking her body, loops back, and does it again. The angle of that run is the direction. Straight up means fly toward the sun. Sixty degrees to the left, means sixty degrees left of the sun. And the waggle's length is the distance. A waggle of about two and a half seconds, means flowers over a mile and a half away. Cracking that code won Karl von Frisch, a Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three. The babies are picky. They need to stay close to ninety-five degrees Fahrenheit. Too cold? Workers shiver their flight muscles, without flapping, and turn into tiny heaters. Too hot? They carry in water, spread it on the comb, and fan it with their wings. As it evaporates, the hive cools down. That's air conditioning, powered by bees. And in winter, they don't hibernate. Below about fifty-seven degrees, they pull into a tight ball around the queen, and burn honey to make heat. That's why they store all that honey. It's their winter fuel. So no single bee knows the plan. Each one just follows simple rules. But put sixty thousand together, and you get something that acts like one giant animal. Next up, why does cilantro taste like soap, to some people?

package.title: Why Do Pigeons Bob Their Heads 5 Times a Second? 🐦
package.description:
Why do pigeons bob their heads when they walk? The head thrusts forward, then holds still in space while the body catches up, which keeps the bird's view of the world steady, and a 1978 treadmill experiment showed the bobbing stops when the surroundings don't move.

package.pinned_comment: Next time you see a pigeon, watch the head: can you catch it standing still?
package.script: Pigeon heads never bob, you've been watching them freeze in midair. Watch one walk, the head shoots forward, about two inches. That's the thrust. Then it stops dead, locked in place, while the body walks underneath it. That's the hold. Then forward again, five to eight times every second. But why bother? In nineteen seventy-eight, scientists in Canada put a pigeon on a treadmill. Its legs kept walking, but the world around it stayed still, and the bobbing stopped. So it isn't about balance, it's about what the bird sees. Holding its head still keeps the view steady, like a camera on a tripod, while the world slides past. Chickens and cranes do it too. So next time you see a pigeon, watch the head. Is it bobbing, or standing still?
key_facts: The head thrusts forward about 2 inches relative to the body, then holds still in space while the body moves forward (Michael Land via Live Science; Journal of Comparative Physiology A 2007 via Snopes).
This happens on average five to eight times a second while walking (Aaron Blaisdell via Live Science).

In 1978, researchers at Queen's University in Canada found the bobbing stopped when a pigeon walked on a treadmill with stationary surroundings, pointing to a visual response rather than balance (Live Science, Snopes).
Chickens and cranes also head-bob (Snopes).

package.pinned_comment: Which cheese has the best pull on your pizza?
package.script: Your pizza cheese hides a protein net, you've never seen. Long proteins called casein, are tied together by tiny calcium bonds, with fat and water stuck in the gaps. Cold, that net is stiff. Warm it up, and the fat melts first, then the bonds loosen. Now the strands slide past each other, without letting go. Mozzarella has an extra trick. Makers dunk the curd in hot water, around 70 to 80 degrees Celsius, then pull and fold it like dough, lining the proteins up in long fibers. Old cheese is different. As it ages, enzymes snip those strands, so it melts, but it won't stretch. Ricotta barely melts at all, its proteins are locked with permanent bonds. So a cheese pull is a net, bending but not breaking. Which cheese has the best pull on your pizza?

Mozzarella curd is stretched in water at 70 to 80 C, aligning casein into parallel fibres (Cheese Scientist)
With ageing, enzymes snip casein, so cheese melts more easily but stretches less (Scientific American)

package.title: Why Does Cilantro Taste Like Soap to 1 in 8 People?
package.description:
Why does cilantro taste like soap to some people and fresh to others? See how aldehydes, the OR6A2 smell gene, a surprisingly tiny genetic effect and what you grew up eating all shape the soapy cilantro taste, plus the crushing trick that can soften it.

package.pinned_comment: Team fresh or team soap: what does cilantro taste like to you?
package.script: Your cilantro tastes like soap, to one in eight people, and you might be one. Same leaf, same taco. You get something fresh and lemony. Your friend gets a mouthful of dish soap. So who's right? Weirdly, you both are. And the answer starts in your nose. People have used this herb for thousands of years, all the way back to the Babylonians. And the haters have been loud. Before soap was the go-to insult, people said it smelled like bedbugs. Chef Julia Child once said, she'd pick it out of her food, and throw it on the floor. So how many people really dislike it? One Canadian study asked nearly fourteen hundred young adults. Dislike ran from just three percent, all the way up to twenty-one percent, depending on family background. And some of the lowest numbers came from people with Hispanic and South Asian roots, whose cooking uses cilantro all the time. Now, let's zoom in on one leaf. That smell is a big mix of chemicals, and some of the main ones are called aldehydes. Picture a long chain of carbon atoms, with one little oxygen on the end. One of them, called decenal, gets described as soapy, fatty and pungent. Here's the twist. Soap makers use aldehydes too. Cilantro and soap really do share a family of smells. Scientists still aren't sure which exact molecule is to blame. So why does only your friend notice? Scientists suspect this is mostly about smell, not taste. When you chew, scents float up the back of your throat, and into your nose. Up there, you've got hundreds of kinds of smell sensors. Think of them as tiny locks, and every scent molecule as a key. In twenty twelve, researchers at twenty-three and me, looked at the DNA of about twenty-five thousand people. They asked one question. Does cilantro taste like soap to you? And they found one tiny spot in the DNA, right next to a cluster of smell genes. One of those genes is called O R six A two, and it builds a lock that's great at catching aldehydes. Some people's noses may pick up that soapy note, a lot more loudly. Case closed, right? Not quite. Here's the number nobody expects. That spot explains only about half a percent of who tastes soap and who doesn't. Half of one percent! Another twin study turned up more genes, including some linked to bitter taste. So there's no single soap gene. It's a small nudge, mixed with everything else about you. Like what you ate growing up. Remember those low numbers? If cilantro was in your food from day one, you've had a lot of practice. The lead researcher said this isn't like your height. You aren't stuck with it. Scientists say eating it again and again, can slowly soften the soap. And there's a kitchen trick. Crush the leaves. Crushing releases enzymes, that break those soapy aldehydes into milder smells. That's why food scientists suggest starting with cilantro pesto. So next time your friend picks it out of the salsa, go easy on them. They aren't being picky. Their nose is finding something real, that yours might be missing. Next up, how do dolphins sleep without drowning?

The SNP explains only about 0.5% of the variance in perceiving soapy taste; the paper says dislike is suspected, not proven, to be odor driven
Mauer & El-Sohemy 2012 (Flavour), via NBC: nearly 1,400 Canadian young adults; dislike 3% (Middle Eastern) to 21% (East Asian), Hispanic 4%, South Asian 7%; early exposure likely helps

Julia Child on Larry King (2002, via Tasting Table): she'd pick it out and throw it on the floor. Described as smelling of bedbugs before 'soapy' (Charles Spence, Live Science). Babylonian use (Gastropod)

package.script:
Your throat slams shut thirty-five milliseconds into every hiccup.
It starts down here, in your diaphragm,
the big muscle under your lungs.
Normally, it moves smoothly,
pulling in air every time you breathe.
But eat too fast, or gulp a fizzy drink,
and your stomach swells right below it.
Then a hiccup center in your brainstem fires,
and the diaphragm jerks down, all at once.
Air rushes in,
but only for a split second.
Your vocal cords snap shut,
and the air smacks right into them.
That's the hic!
Babies even do it before they're born.
And scientists still aren't sure why.
One idea is it helps clear air from the stomach.
Another says it's just a leftover reflex.
So the next time your throat slams shut,
what's your go-to trick for stopping it?

The glottis closes about 35 milliseconds after the respiratory muscles activate, which makes the sound
Triggers include eating too fast and carbonated drinks, which swell the stomach
Fetuses hiccup in the womb
The purpose is unsettled: ideas include clearing stomach air and a vestigial reflex

package.pinned_comment: How many seconds can you go without blinking? Tell me your record!
package.script: You go blind fifteen thousand times every day. Why can't you tell? It's called blinking. Each blink lasts about a tenth of a second. The clear front of your eye has no blood vessels, so it relies on a film of tears instead. That film has three parts: mucus, water, and oil. Every blink wipes on a fresh coat, like a tiny windshield wiper, and sweeps dust toward your eye's drain. So why doesn't the world go black? Scientists scanned people's brains during blinks, and found parts of the visual system go quiet, right as your eyelid comes down. Your brain deletes the blackout, before you can ever see it. Altogether, your eyes are shut for about half an hour every day. So how many seconds can you go without blinking? Tell me your record.

A blink lasts about 100-150 ms
Tear film spreads with each blink: mucus, water, oil; cornea has no direct blood supply
Brain activity in visual areas is suppressed during blinks (Bristow 2005; Golan 2016)

package.pinned_comment: What's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?
package.script: You just ate molecules, your bread never had. That's what toast is. So why does it taste so much better? Bread holds two key ingredients: sugars, and amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Normally, they mostly ignore each other. But in the toaster, dry heat drives water out of the surface. Then, at around a hundred and forty degrees Celsius, they start reacting. It's called the Maillard reaction, first described in nineteen twelve. It builds hundreds of new flavor molecules, nutty, roasty, toasty. And the brown? That's melanoidins, big brown molecules. The inside stays cooler and wetter, so it stays soft and pale. Push it too far, though, and it burns to bitter black char. So what's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?

package.title: Why Do Cows Spend 8 Hours a Day Chewing Burps? 🐄
package.description:
Why do cows burp up their lunch and chew it again? A cow's one stomach has four compartments, and microbes in the giant rumen ferment tough grass that cows can't digest alone.

package.pinned_comment: Would you chew your lunch twice, yes or no?
package.script: Cows burp up their lunch on purpose, and you'd never guess why. Grass is really hard to digest. Its walls are made of cellulose, and cows can't break that down alone. So one stomach has four rooms. Room one is the rumen, a vat holding up to forty gallons. It's packed with tiny microbes, and they ferment the grass. Room two, the honeycomb, sorts the pieces. Big chunks go back up her throat, as a soggy ball called cud. She chews it again, for about eight hours a day. Fine mush slides into room three, where water gets squeezed out. Room four is the true stomach, full of acid, like yours. All that fermenting makes gas, hundreds of litres of methane a day, and she burps it out. So, would you chew your lunch twice?

topic.title: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?

package.title: How Do Dolphins Sleep 8 Hours a Day Without Drowning?
package.description:
How do dolphins sleep without drowning when every breath is a choice? They rest one half of the brain at a time with one eye open, and in a 2012 test a dolphin stayed alert for 15 days straight.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-do-whales-and-dolphin/
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121017181244.htm
https://www.mpg.de/10673637/frigatebirds-sleep

Animated in the 16-Bit Pixel Odyssey style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: If you could keep half your brain awake while the other half slept, what would you use the awake half for?
package.script: You sleep with your whole brain. Dolphins can't: one full nap and they'd drown. So how do they sleep eight hours a day? You pass out at night, and your body keeps breathing without asking. A dolphin doesn't get that deal. Dolphins are mammals, so they breathe air, like you. But every breath is a choice. The blowhole on top of its head is a flap of skin, and scientists think it opens on purpose, not automatically. The dolphin swims up, opens it, breathes out and in, then snaps it shut. So picture one falling fully asleep at sea. Nobody's at the controls. The air stops coming, and the water's right there. So how do you rest a brain that can never switch off? You switch off half of it. It's called unihemispheric sleep, which is a big word for one side at a time. One half of the brain drops into slow, deep waves. The other half stays awake, at low power, running the breathing, and watching for trouble. And you can actually see it from the outside. When the left half sleeps, the right eye closes. When the right half sleeps, the left eye closes. After about two hours, they swap. Each side gets roughly four hours across the day, so a dolphin sleeps about a third of its day, around eight hours. So what does that look like? Two moves. The first is called logging. The dolphin floats at the surface, barely moving, looking exactly like a log. The second is slow swimming, in big circles. In one study of pool dolphins, most of them circled counterclockwise. Breathing slows down too, from around ten breaths a minute, to as few as three. And the open eye has a job. When two dolphins rest side by side, it's the eye that faces the partner. Now, you'd expect half asleep to mean half useless. Researchers tested that in twenty twelve. They had two dolphins spot targets with echolocation, continuously, day and night. Both kept going for five days, with no signs of getting tired. Then the female kept going, for fifteen days. Fifteen, with near-perfect accuracy. Nobody knows how much longer she could've gone, because the test just stopped. So scientists think this trick isn't only about breathing. It may be about staying alert, too. Then there are the newborns. A baby dolphin rests while its mother swims, getting towed along in her slipstream. She can't stop swimming for the first several weeks. One study said mothers and calves barely sleep for a month. Other researchers watched closely, and saw eyes closing during swim rest, so scientists are still arguing about that one. And dolphins aren't alone. Mallard ducks at the edge of a group, keep one eye open, pointed away from the others. Frigatebirds sleep while flying, on trips of up to ten days, averaging just forty-two minutes a day. Back on land, they sleep over twelve hours. So half a brain is a trick nature keeps reusing. One side rests, one side breathes, and nobody drowns. Next question: what actually happens when a jellyfish stings you? It has no brain at all, so who gives the order?
key_facts: Dolphins are conscious breathers; the blowhole flap is thought to open under voluntary control
Unihemispheric sleep: one hemisphere sleeps and the opposite eye closes; sides swap after about two hours
Bottlenose dolphins sleep about 33% of the day by EEG, about four hours per hemisphere
Resting breaths fall from 8-12 to 3-7 a minute
2012 PLOS ONE: two dolphins echolocated for 5 days with no fatigue; the female went 15 days with near-perfect accuracy

package.pinned_comment: Which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?
package.script: Why does your foot lose signal when you sit on it? Most people blame blood flow, but scientists call that mostly a myth. The real culprit is a nerve. Think of it like a garden hose, carrying signals instead of water. Messages run from your foot to your brain. So you cross your legs. That pressure pinches the nerve, like stepping on the hose. Signals get blocked, or come through scrambled. Your brain hears almost nothing, so your foot goes numb. Then you stand up. The nerve starts working again, but it isn't smooth yet. Messy signals rush through, and your brain probably reads them as tiny prickles. Those are pins and needles, and they usually fade in minutes. So which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?

package.pinned_comment: Do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else in your house?
package.script: How does a mosquito find you in the pitch dark? Your breath. Only females hunt you, because they need blood to make eggs. Every time you breathe out, you leave a trail of carbon dioxide. Scientists think she can smell it from up to fifty meters away, about half a football field. She follows that invisible trail. Closer in, she picks up your body odor. In daylight, she'd spot you from about fifteen meters, but tonight, that's no help. So here's her secret weapon. Tiny pits on her antenna tips sense the infrared heat your skin gives off, from about seventy centimeters away. In one lab study, adding that heat doubled how hard mosquitoes searched. Breath, then smell, then heat. And she lands. So tell me: do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else?

Researchers hypothesize mosquitoes smell a CO2 plume from 10 to 50 meters (Caltech 2015, model-based).

Aedes aegypti detect thermal infrared up to about 70 cm via antenna-tip peg-in-pit structures (Nature 2024).

package.title: How Do Bacteria Turn Milk Into Yogurt in 5 Hours? 🥛

How is yogurt made? Two kinds of bacteria eat the lactose in warm milk and make lactic acid, and at about pH 4.6 the milk proteins clump into a soft net that turns thin milk thick.

package.pinned_comment: Would you still eat yogurt, knowing bacteria made it?
package.script: Your yogurt is milk that two kinds of bacteria soured in about five hours. First, the milk gets heated, to around two hundred degrees Fahrenheit. That changes its proteins, so they can set together later. Then it cools to about a hundred and ten, and two kinds of bacteria get stirred in. One looks like chains of tiny beads, the other like little rods. They only want one thing: lactose, the sugar in milk. For about five hours, they eat it, and make lactic acid. Then comes the magic number: four point six. At that pH, floating proteins clump, into a soft, wobbly net. That net traps the liquid, and thin milk turns thick. That tangy taste? That's the acid too. So tell me, would you still eat it, knowing bacteria made it?

package.title: How Can a Jellyfish Sting in a Millionth of a Second?
package.description:

tags: what happens when a jellyfish stings you
package.pinned_comment: Have you ever been stung by a jellyfish, and what did it feel like?
package.script: A jellyfish can sting you, in under a millionth of a second, without a brain, and you'd never see it coming. So what actually happens, when one of them stings you? First, meet the animal. Jellyfish have been drifting through the ocean, for more than 500 million years. And they've never had a brain. They also have no heart, no bones, and no blood. What they have instead, is a simple net of nerves, spread through a soft, see-through body. So when a jellyfish stings you, it isn't angry. It isn't even really aware of you. Most of them just drift, and let their tentacles do the work. Now zoom in on one tentacle. It's covered in thousands of tiny stinging cells. And inside each cell sits a capsule, called a nematocyst. Several of them could fit, across a single human hair. Packed inside that capsule, is a long, hollow thread, coiled up like a spring, with a sharp tip waiting at the front. Think of it as a loaded harpoon, sitting in a bath of venom. The pressure in there is huge, about 150 times normal air pressure. That's dozens of times stronger, than the air in a car tire. So what sets it off? Each cell has a tiny trigger on the outside. Bump it, or hit it with the right chemicals, and the lid pops open. Seawater rushes in, the pressure takes over, and the harpoon fires. No brain tells it to. The cell mostly acts on its own. Now here's the part that's hard to believe. In 2006, scientists filmed this, in hydra, a tiny relative of the jellyfish. Their camera shot over a million frames per second. And the first part of the shot, was over in just 700 nanoseconds. That's seven ten-millionths of a second. The tip hit up to five million g's. people tend to black out at around six. And a mantis shrimp's famous punch, reaches about ten thousand. Because that tip is so tiny, the pressure where it lands, is in the range of a bullet. It's strong enough to pierce a crab's shell. So what happens in your skin? After the tip punches in, the thread turns itself inside out, and the capsule squeezes venom through it. Some of those toxins punch holes in cells. Others go after nerves. One cell alone does almost nothing. But brushing a tentacle sets off thousands, all at once, and that's the sudden burn you feel. package.pinned_comment: What's the spiciest chili that's ever fooled you?
package.script:
Chili isn't hot.
You've been fooled every single time.
Put one in the fridge,
and it still burns.
Your tongue is covered in tiny heat alarms.
They stay quiet,
until something hits about forty-three degrees Celsius,
that's a hundred and nine Fahrenheit.
But chili carries a molecule called capsaicin,
and it fits that alarm like a key.
The alarm goes off at body temperature,
and yells to your brain: this is burning!
So you even start to sweat,
but nothing's actually heating up.
Water won't save you,
capsaicin won't mix with it.
Milk's protein, casein, wraps it up,
and carries it away.

topic.title: Why do your nails keep growing when your arms stopped?

package.title: Why Do Nails Grow 3mm a Month Forever?
package.description:
Why do your fingernails keep growing your whole life when your bones stopped growing in your teens? Growth plates in long bones turn to solid bone after puberty, but the nail matrix under your cuticle keeps making new cells, about 3 mm of fingernail a month.

package.pinned_comment: Which grows faster: your fingernails or your toenails?
package.script: Your nails never stop growing, but your arms stopped years ago. So why does one keep going? It starts with your bones. Near each end of a long bone sits a soft strip called a growth plate. It keeps adding new bone, so your arms get longer. But by your late teens, that strip turns to solid bone. The plate closes, and your arms stop for good. Nails work differently. Under your cuticle hides the nail matrix, a tiny factory that never shuts down. It keeps making new cells, pushing the older ones forward. Those cells harden and die, which is why clipping doesn't hurt. Fingernails grow about three millimeters a month, so a whole new nail takes around six months. So which grows faster: your fingernails, or your toenails?

Growth plates ossify and close after puberty, around the late teens
The nail matrix under the cuticle produces new cells throughout life, pushing older ones forward
Nail plate cells harden (keratinize) and are dead, so clipping is painless
Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month; a whole fingernail regrows in about 6 months; toenails grow slower

package.script: Koalas eat poison leaves you'd never survive. So why only eucalyptus? Eucalyptus leaves are tough, low in nutrients, and toxic to most animals. So koalas get the trees to themselves. package.script:
Your stomach acid dissolves metal,
so how does your stomach survive it,
three times a day?
The acid can drop to pH one point five.
Strong enough to eat through zinc,
and turn a steak to mush.
But your stomach has three tricks.
Trick one: a thick blanket of mucus,
loaded with bicarbonate,
basically baking soda.
So right against the wall,
the acid gets neutralized.
Trick two: pepsin, the meat-eating enzyme,
is made switched off.
It only turns on out in the acid,
away from your cells.
Trick three: your lining sheds around half a million cells,
every minute,
and rebuilds itself every few days.
So damage gets replaced before it spreads.
Your stomach isn't acid-proof.
It just heals faster than it melts.
Which trick would you want: the slime, the switch, or the shedding?
key_facts: Stomach acid can reach about pH 1.5 (normal range roughly 1.5-3.5)
A mucus layer rich in bicarbonate neutralizes acid right at the stomach wall
Pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen and is activated by acid in the stomach cavity
The lining sheds roughly 500,000 cells a minute and renews itself every few days (about 3-5 days)

package.title: Why Can Bare Hands Hold Shut a 3,700-Pound Crocodile Bite?
package.description:
A saltwater crocodile has the strongest bite ever measured, about 3,700 pounds of force, yet its jaws can be held shut by hand because the muscles that open them are tiny. We look inside the crocodile jaw, the bite force record, how wildlife handlers use rubber bands and tape, the touch sensors that make croc jaws more sensitive than fingertips, and how alligators replace each tooth up to 50 times.

Sources:

https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2012/11/alligators-and-crocodiles

package.script:
Why can your bare hands hold shut
the strongest bite ever measured,
3,700 pounds of crocodile?
It sounds impossible, but it's true.
Let's open up the most lopsided jaw in nature.
Back in 2012, a team of scientists
set out to measure every crocodile on Earth.
All 23 living species,
from tiny caimans to giant gharials.
They wrestled each one
into biting down on a padded force meter.
The winner was the saltwater crocodile.
One big male bit down with about 3,700 pounds of force.
That's more than sixteen thousand newtons.
For comparison, you chew a steak
with maybe 150 to 200 pounds.
Lions, tigers and hyenas
land somewhere around 1,000.
So the saltie bites more than three times harder
than the big cats.
So where does all that power come from?
Look at the back of a crocodile's head.
Those big bulging cheeks aren't fat.
They're almost all jaw-closing muscle,
packed around the hinge
and pulling the lower jaw up like giant rubber bands.
Now look for the muscles that open the jaw.
They're tiny.
A thin little strap
that just tugs the jaw back down.
And that makes sense for how a crocodile eats.
It lies still in the water,
then snaps shut and holds on.
Clamping needs huge force.
Opening only has to lift the jaw's own weight.
So evolution poured almost everything
into closing.
That's the trick behind the bare-hands myth.
Once the jaws are already shut,
the weak opening muscles have to push
against your grip,
and they lose.
Wildlife handlers use this every day.
They loop a strong rubber band around the snout,
or wrap it with a few turns of tape,
and the crocodile simply can't open up.
But please, never try this yourself.
Getting the mouth shut is the dangerous part,
and that tail is all muscle too.
Here's the most surprising part.
Those crushing jaws are also incredibly gentle.
Look closely at a crocodile's face
and you'll see thousands of tiny bumps.
Each bump is a touch sensor,
and scientists found they're more sensitive
than your own fingertips.
They can feel a ripple
from a single drop of water.
They help a crocodile sense prey in the dark,
and they let a mother crocodile
carry her newly hatched babies in her mouth
without hurting a single one.
And then there are the teeth.
An alligator has about 80,
and each one can be replaced up to 50 times
over its long life.
A new tooth is always waiting underneath
the old one.
Scientists are studying how they do it,
hoping it might one day help people
regrow lost teeth.
So the crocodile's jaw is a one-way machine.
Record-breaking power to close,
barely any to open,
and a touch as soft as a fingertip.
Next time, why do porcupine quills
get stuck in you and refuse to come out?

You chew a steak with about 150-200 psi; lions, tigers and hyenas around 1,000 psi (National Geographic)
Croc jaws are mostly jaw-closing muscle; the opening muscles are weak, so hands, rubber bands or tape can hold them shut
Integumentary sensory organs on croc jaws are more sensitive to pressure than human fingertips; used to carry hatchlings (Leitch & Catania 2012)
An alligator can replace each of its ~80 teeth up to 50 times (Smithsonian)

package.script:
Pandas waste eighty-three percent of the bamboo they eat.
Here's why you never see it.
Inside, a panda has a meat-eater's gut,
built just like a bear's:
short, simple intestines,
and no cow-style stomach chambers.
So bamboo rushes straight through,
and most of it comes out in less than a day.
So pandas eat for up to fourteen hours a day,
crunching up to thirty-eight kilos of bamboo.
And they save energy like a phone on low battery.
Their thyroid runs slow,
their brain and liver are small,
and they nap a lot.
A panda burns barely forty percent of the energy
you'd expect for its size.
Scientists think it all started
when their ancestors lost a gene
for tasting meat's savory flavor.
Could you eat just one food every day, like a panda?

package.title: How Do 6,000 Bird Species Sleep on Twigs Without Falling?
package.description:
Why don't birds fall off branches when they sleep? See how a perching bird's leg tendons curl its toes around a twig, why songbirds have a zip-tie-like tendon lock, and why sleeping starlings turned out to be mostly balancing.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: When a bird dozes on a wire, do you think it's gripping or just balancing?
package.script: A sleeping bird never falls off its branch. You'd never guess why. When a bird bends its legs, tendons behind its ankles pull tight, and that curls the toes around the twig. In songbirds, tiny bumps on those tendons catch on ridges, like a zip tie, so the grip holds with little effort. To let go, it just stands up. But here's the twist. When scientists filmed sleeping starlings, their legs weren't bent enough to lock. They were mostly balancing, probably helped by a balance sensor near their hips, not just their ears. Many birds even sleep with half their brain, one eye open for danger. That's how perching birds, over half of all bird species, nap safely in the trees. So when a bird dozes on a wire, is it gripping, or just balancing?
key_facts: Bending the leg pulls flexor tendons behind the ankle tight and curls the toes around the perch (Ornithology.com, Birds Outside My Window)
Songbirds have ridges/pads between tendon and sheath that help lock the grip (Gill, Ornithology, via Birds Outside My Window; ScienceABC)
Straightening the leg relaxes the tendon and opens the toes (Ornithology.com)
A 2012 study of sleeping European starlings found legs not bent enough to engage the lock; they balanced (Galton & Shepherd 2012, via ScienceABC)
A lumbosacral balance organ near the hips is thought to aid balance (ScienceABC, Juneau Empire; hedged 'probably')
Many birds sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time and one eye open (ScienceABC, Rattenborg)
Perching birds (passerines) are more than half of all bird species, over 6,000 species (UTK 2019, Encyclopedia.com)

package.script: You've never seen a flamingo eat right-side up. It feeds with its head upside down, because its beak is built backwards. Most birds have a big top beak, and a smaller bottom one. package.description:

package.pinned_comment: Which baby tooth did you lose first: a front one on the bottom, like most kids, or something else?
package.script:
Every baby tooth you ever lost,
was secretly eaten.
By what?
Kids have twenty baby teeth.
Adults have thirty-two.
But a tiny jaw can't fit big adult teeth,
so the new ones wait,
hidden in the bone underneath.
Around age six,
an adult tooth starts pushing up.
That pressure wakes up special cells,
called odontoclasts.
They dissolve the baby tooth's root,
bit by bit.
No root means nothing holding on,
so it wobbles,
and pops out.
That's why a lost baby tooth,
looks like it has no root at all.
It got eaten.
Then the adult tooth slides into the gap.
By about age twelve,
most baby teeth are gone.
So which of yours got eaten first?

Permanent teeth develop in the jawbone beneath the baby teeth
Pressure from the erupting adult tooth activates odontoclasts that resorb the baby tooth's root

Most baby teeth are lost by about age 12

topic.title: Why do your knuckles crack?

package.title: Why Do Your Knuckles Crack? 🫧
package.description:
Why do knuckles crack? Pulling a finger joint apart drops the pressure in its fluid, so dissolved gas forms a bubble with a pop, and it takes about 20 minutes before that knuckle can crack again.

package.pinned_comment: How many times have you cracked your knuckles today? Be honest 👀
package.script:
Your knuckle crack is actually a gas bubble,
and it can't happen again for twenty minutes.
Every finger joint sits in a tiny capsule,
filled with a slippery fluid.
That fluid has gas dissolved in it,
like a soda with the cap on.
When you pull or bend the joint,
the capsule stretches,
and the pressure inside drops.
The gas rushes out of the fluid,
and a bubble forms, with a pop!
In 2015, scientists filmed it in an MRI scanner,
and saw the bubble appear right at the crack.
Try that knuckle again, and... nothing.
The bubble needs about twenty minutes
to dissolve back into the fluid.
And no, studies say it won't give you arthritis.
One doctor cracked only his left hand's knuckles
for sixty years,
and both hands stayed the same.
So, how many bubbles have you made today?
key_facts: Finger joints are wrapped in a capsule of synovial fluid that holds dissolved gas
Pulling the joint apart drops the pressure and a gas cavity forms with the crack (2015 University of Alberta MRI study, Kawchuk et al.)
It takes about 20 minutes before the same knuckle can crack again
Dr. Donald Unger cracked only his left hand's knuckles for about 60 years and found no arthritis in either hand (2009 Ig Nobel)

topic.title: Your Taste Buds Explained in Simple Words: how taste buds work and why they die every ten days

package.title: Why Your Taste Buds Die Every 10 Days
package.description:
How do taste buds work, why is the tongue map a myth, and why do your taste cells get replaced about every 10 days? A simple explainer of papillae, taste receptors, the five basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami), why smell makes most of flavor, and the catfish with 175,000 taste buds.

Sources:
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/24684-taste-buds
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue_map
https://www.livescience.com/32970-what-animal-has-the-best-sense-of-taste.html

package.pinned_comment: Were you taught the tongue map in school? Tell me which flavor you were told lives on the tip!
package.script: Your taste buds die every ten days, and nobody ever told you why. Right now, thousands of tiny sensors are tasting your own spit. So what are they, how do they work, and what about that tongue map from school? Let's start with the map. You've probably seen it. Sweet on the tip, bitter at the back, sour and salty on the sides. It's a myth. In nineteen oh one, a German scientist named David Hanig found that some spots were just a tiny bit more sensitive. Then in nineteen forty two, his graph got redrawn, and people read it the wrong way. The truth? Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can taste all five flavors. So where are the taste buds? Stick out your tongue in a mirror. Those little bumps are not taste buds. They're called papillae, and most taste buds hide inside them, along the sides of each bump. An adult has somewhere between two thousand and ten thousand taste buds. A few even live on the roof of your mouth and down in your throat. Now zoom in on one bud. It looks a bit like a tiny onion, packed with fifty to one hundred fifty taste cells. At the top there's a little opening, called a taste pore. When you eat, food dissolves in your spit, and those molecules slip into the pore. Each taste cell has receptors on its tip, like locks waiting for the right key. Sugar fits the sweet lock. Salt slips through its own little channel. When a key fits, the cell fires a signal down a nerve, and your brain says, sweet! And here's the clever part. Each of the five tastes has a job. Sweet means energy. Salty means minerals your body needs. Sour can mean unripe, or spoiled. Bitter is a warning, because lots of poisons taste bitter. And umami means protein. That fifth taste was found in nineteen oh eight, by a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda. He wondered why seaweed soup tasted so rich, and found the answer was glutamate. But taste is only half the story. Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You can tell it's sweet, but not what flavor it is. That's because most of what we call flavor actually comes from smell. And some animals put us to shame. A catfish can have up to one hundred seventy five thousand taste buds, all over its body. It's basically a swimming tongue. Now, back to that hook. Your taste cells work in a wet, rough place, getting scraped by crunchy food, and burned by hot soup. So your body replaces them, about every ten days. That's why a burned tongue feels normal again so fast. Every bite you take, thousands of brand new taste cells are on the job. Next time, why do some people get carsick, while others feel totally fine?
key_facts: Adults have about 2,000 to 10,000 taste buds, each with 50 to 150 taste receptor cells; taste cells are replaced roughly every 10 days (Cleveland Clinic)
Most taste buds sit in papillae (fungiform, circumvallate, foliate); a few are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat (Cleveland Clinic)
Tongue map myth: David P. Hanig's 1901 paper found only minute threshold differences; Edwin Boring's 1942 redrawn graphs were misread; all tastes are sensed across the tongue (Wikipedia: Tongue map)
Umami identified by chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 from kombu seaweed broth; the molecule is glutamate (BrainFacts)
Large catfish can have up to 175,000 taste buds, all over the body (Live Science)

package.script: A 500-kilo horse can sleep standing up, and you'd never guess why it doesn't fall. The trick is called the stay apparatus. Tendons and ligaments brace its legs, so the joints lock with almost no muscle effort. In a back leg, the kneecap hooks over a bump on the thigh bone, like a latch clicking shut. The other back leg gets to rest, and every so often it swaps sides. But there's a catch. Dreaming sleep, called REM, relaxes every muscle, and that unlocks the legs. So for REM, a horse has to lie down, about thirty to forty-five minutes a day, often while a buddy stands guard. Miss it for a week or so, and its knees can buckle mid-nap. So, could you sleep standing up, or would you fall flat on your face?
key_facts: The stay apparatus is a system of tendons and ligaments that stabilizes the joints of the forelimbs and hindlimbs so horses can doze standing (SmartPak, TheHorse)

In the hind leg the kneecap (patella) hooks over the medial ridge of the femur to lock the stifle; the horse rests the other hind leg and swaps (standard equine anatomy; TheHorse on the stay apparatus)
REM sleep relaxes all muscle tone, including the stay apparatus, so horses must lie down (sternal or lateral) for it (TheHorse, SmartPak)
Horses need about 30 (SmartPak) to 40-45 (TheHorse) minutes of REM per day; script says 'about thirty to forty-five minutes'
In wild herds one horse often stays awake on watch while others lie down (TheHorse, SmartPak); script hedges with 'often'
REM deprivation lasting more than a week or so can make horses drift into REM standing and collapse, with bowing knees (Houpt and Greening via TheHorse)
Average horse weight ~500 kg (common figure for a riding horse)
